If you are asked about awareness, whatever source that awareness has, whether you've seen the statement, whether you heard about it, whether you typed anything out about it, everything should then be part of an answer to such a question. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two further questions on this, Mr. Tomas, if I may. Whether you saw the statement or not, you must have known, mustn't you, that Mr. Alija was in custody by the 3rd of September?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if somebody had told me that, but nobody did. I didn't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's obvious from the document you signed on the 11th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that now that I'm looking at the document, I see that this is indeed the case. At the time I did not think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So let me ask you one further question then on this part of the evidence. You've told us just a moment ago that your role in this interview was to just help compile the document because the interview was conducted exclusively in Albanian. Is that true, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Why was it conducted in Albanian and not Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you an assumption. I suppose that the person interviewed did not have the required knowledge of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you read the last three lines of this statement, please, on the 11th to us. The last two sentences will do. Just read them aloud into the transcript, if you will.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have nothing further to state regarding the above. My statement was taken in the Serbian language, which I understand, and it contains all that I have said. It was read back to me aloud and with my signature I accept it in its entirety as my own." May I just add the following. All the statements we took were drafted in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not that --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the person interviewed could have known -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, perhaps not, in fact, because I'm asking you for a specific series of questions and answers, and you're more than welcome to answer any questions. Mr. Kearney is more than welcome to re-examine you, but I'm under some pressure of time. The question I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to my colleague, but this witness was in the middle of answering a question. I don't think it's appropriate to stop him while he's trying to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to focus the witness on the question that's being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Mr. Kearney objects, we'll allow the witness to add what he intended to add. Please add what you intended to add, Mr. Tomas, to your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say this: All the statements taken were taken in the Serbian language. This is the customary formulation placed at the end of a statement; namely, what I just read in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The passage that I'm interested in is the fact -- the reference to the penultimate sentence to the fact that the witness is recorded as saying that he understands Serbian. You've given evidence just a few moments ago that as far as you were able to recall it he did not understand Serbian. What was the position, did he or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, what I meant primarily was that he did not speak Serbian. One can have passive knowledge of the language. Many people from the territory, if they were conscripts, most of them understood Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Can I -- in those circumstances, can I just ask you, please, to turn to tab 16. I'm moving to another topic at this point. I want to do this relatively briefly. The document that I'm showing you behind tab 16 is -- just give me one moment. I'm sorry, I've given you the wrong reference. I should have given you tab 12. The document behind tab 12 is a list of minutes for the Joint Command for Kosovo. And I wanted to just ask you one or two quick questions about these, if I may. These record information being supplied back to a Joint Command consisting of the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic; representatives of the MUP, the VJ, and the RDB, amongst others. If we could just look at the first page there there's a list of names of those who were members of the Joint Command and whose comments appear in these minutes. And you know, I think, don't you, Nikola Sainovic and Zoran Andjelkovic, because in your statement you say both of them attended the scene of the canal on the very afternoon of the reconnaissance mission on the 8th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two of them were present. Andjelkovic came first and was followed by Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And they managed to get there within a very short time of your discovery of the canal; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot trace back the chronology of the events. I can only tell you that Mr. Andjelkovic came first and Mr. Sainovic next. I can't tell you when exactly that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you know who David Gajic is, don't you, number 7, because he was the assistant chief of the RDB, the organisation you worked for. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was stationed in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. He was the -- the head of the RDB in Kosovo, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was at the head of the Kosovo service. It's just that I'm not sure that this was the proper name it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he reported to a man called Jovica Stanisic, is that correct, the head of the RDB as a whole?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic reported directly to President Slobodan Milosevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only presume that this was the case. It was too far removed from me in hierarchical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you turn to page 82. If you look at the bottom right-hand corner, there's some numbers there. Could you turn to page 82 -- no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's going to be difficult for the witness to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is an entry for the 1st of September under the name of Mr. Muric. Perhaps, if I can simply -- rather than trying to find it in the manuscript version, perhaps given the time if I can draw your attention to it, Mr. Tomas. These minutes record that on the 8th [sic] of September a Mr. Muric is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're now on what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this is page 82 of 164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I believe that's the 1st of September, counsel, not the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did I say the 8th? I meant to say the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's corrected because on the next page is it is 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you, please, then restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In these minutes, on the 1st of September, there is an entry under the name of Mr. Muric, which says as follows: "Secondly, in Glodjane, the priority is also to be given to the examination of Radonjic lake and a possible deployment of divers teams. The evidence for crimes is to be delivered, or transferred, to a higher level." I wonder if you can shed any light on why it was thought that divers were required before these interviews that you conducted on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm qualified to explain this. Since this is unknown to me, I can only give you my interpretation of it; that's to say, that they already had intelligence to the effect that there was something there, and then followed on from that point. I have to say that this is quite unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this sort of meetings is so far removed from me that I'm not qualified to interpret that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that it's operating at a level very similar to yours. Could you turn to -- I'm sorry. Can we turn to page 87 of 164. Because on the 4th of September, Mr. Tomas, there is an entry from Mr. Gajic, who was the head of the organisation in Kosovo for which you worked, which records at the fifth bullet point: "In the village of Ratis near Decani, there is a mass graveyard (34 Serbs, 3 Romanies, and 3 Albanians)." Can you shed any light for us on how it might be three days before the interviews you conducted and a day before you went to the canal there could be a record of the number of individuals with that level of detail in Mr. Gajic's information?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on this. I wasn't aware of the existence of such a statement. I don't see how I can account for this, other than that there existed intelligence to that will effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, I'm suggesting to you - and I suggested it to you at the outset - that the authorities for whom you work had been to the canal area and the two men you had in your custody were beaten into signing confessions, in which words were being put into their mouths by you and your colleagues. That's the suggestion I'm making, Mr. Tomas.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I should answer this, I find this statement from the Defence counsel quite unacceptable, since I -- I received the first knowledge of these matters on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Could you turn to tab 16, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'll be corrected if I'm wrong. I don't believe there's any application for protective measures in respect of this witness. Sorry, tab 13 is the -- I've again given you the wrong reference. I do apologise. Tab 13.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man. I know the gentleman. You asked me if I know Mr. Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what's the answer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that he was the head of the criminal department of SUP Gjakove and was in overall charge of the operation of the SUP in the Lake Radoniq canal area.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was one of the persons holding managerial positions in the department in Djakovica. I don't know which particular post. I know that he always joined teams as they attended scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've looked at the video of the 8th of September from start to finish, have you, when the Prosecution showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw clips of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see yourself in any of those clips?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we turn to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Emmerson, there's some confusion. You asked the witness whether he had seen the video from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer of the witness was that he had seen clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The reason I didn't pursue that - and it may be obvious to Your Honour - but the video itself proceeds in clip; in other words, it was being turned on and off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was unclear to me, whether he had seen the whole of it or whether he now says, I have seen only part of it; or the that whole is composed of clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he may not the answer to that, and it may be that the Prosecution can furnish that information in due course, as to what exactly was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you turn to paragraph 13, please, in that statement, Mr. Tomas, 1-3, 13. I'm going to read that into the record for the public purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do it slowly, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's always helpful to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "After the interrogations were finished," and this is a reference to the interrogations of the men concerned. "After the interrogations were finished, I think it was one day before the crime scene investigations started. Members of SUP Djakovica together with at least one detained member of the KLA went to the crime site at Lake Radonjic next to the village of Donji Ratis. This was on the 8th September, 1998. "The name of one KLA person I recall as Bekim Kalimashi. I am not sure if there was another KLA member with the team. I also recall a Catholic person from Ratis who was called 'Toma' and he seemed to be a contact person for one of the services. I am not sure if he was detained like the KLA members. "The SUP team who made the first crime scene" -- I'm sorry, "the first crime site visit at the canal consisted of the following persons: General-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic, chief of public security sector for the MUP Serbia; Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic, deputy chief of security, chief of Gjakove SUP; Dragutin Adamovic, chief of Gjakove state security; Sreten Camovic; crime inspector Goran Mitic; crime inspector Dusan Dragovic; crime technician Nebojsa Avramovic; crime technician Zarko Gazdic. "From the state security, the following members formed part of this team: The late crime inspector Dejan Jovovic; the crime technician Sava Jovanovic, who was in charge for video-recording. Before they reached the actual crime site, they didn't know exactly the location of the killed persons. Based on the interrogations, we assumed that they are in the triangle between the villages of Jablanica and Glodjane and the Lake Radonjic." Now, pausing there for a moment, you agree, I think, don't you, that Dejan Jovovic was part of your reconnaissance party on the 8th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dejan Jovovic was ahead of me, together with Musaj, and I was behind with Zenelj. However, this was left -- he left this bit out in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson. The relevant portions, including this one, will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you agree that Sava Jovanovic was present with you and conducting the video-recording. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is indicated here. I said that the person was the only crime technician from the state security department in Djakovica, and that was precisely the person whose name you read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you can confirm that that is correct, that name is correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was clear. I said that the only crime technician from the department is the person by this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll hear about some of the other people from other witnesses, but you can confirm, as well, that Sreten Camovic was with you as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He walked behind me. He followed behind at some distance with a group of people who walked behind Dejan Jovovic, myself, and some Albanian persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you please confirm or deny that General-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic was on the reconnaissance mission?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I can just confirm about the people whom I know. I can confirm about Sreten Camovic, the crime technician, Dejan Jovovic, and myself, because those are the people I knew at that moment. As for the others, they were not familiar to me. Now, as I read their names, yes, I can have some idea who they are, but at the time I was not paying attention to them because we walked ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now that you know who they were please answer the question: Was Lieutenant-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic with the reconnaissance mission, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that at the time. This is the first time that I am reading in this document that he was there, as was the other general.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you been issued with instructions not to admit that Lieutenant-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic took part in the reconnaissance mission on the 8th? Have you been ordered to write him out of your account?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody gave me any instructions about this, but had I seen that I would have told you. Just like I mentioned the politicians, I would have told you about him. So all I remember were Sainovic and Andjelkovic, people that I was familiar with. As for the others, I didn't know them. I told you about the persons whom I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You know, don't you, Mr. Tomas, from your own knowledge, that Vlastimir Djordjevic has been indicted by this Tribunal and was very recently arrested on allegations that he is one of the principal architects of a plan in March and April of 1999 to dig-up remains of Kosovar Albanians and to conceal them by transporting them to Serbia in an effort to conceal war crimes allegations. You know that is an allegation widely publicised in Serbia against Vlastimir Djordjevic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You know that a refrigerated lorry container with approximately 50 human remains of Kosovar Albanians was found in the River Danube near Kladovo in eastern Serbia in 1999 and that a further container lorry was found in Lake Perucac, and that the bodies from the container lorries were then, after an attempt to burn them, buried at a mass grave adjacent to SAJ barracks near Batajnica. That's something you're aware of, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was publicised in the press, and this is how I know it, from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you know that more than 450 Kosovar Albanian bodies were dug-up from Batajnica, and that the repatriation operation is still going on, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read some of that in the press, but I cannot be sure that I have all of the facts concerning that. I'm now referring to the figures of the victims mentioned by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that caveat. You also know, don't you, from your knowledge, that an official MUP investigation concluded that General-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic had orchestrated that operation in direct consultation with President Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know how could I have learned of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's been widely publicised, I suggest, inside Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, does it make any sense to go with the witness through all the newspaper messages. Well, you've now given three examples. He says I read newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my concern is - and I put the suggestion to the witness - that this witness and others to come have deliberately written General-Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic out of their account of those who attended the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That is an inappropriate question, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this is the question for the witness, I take it. Perhaps you should make clear to Mr. Tomas that that's what you put to him. Mr. Tomas, did you understand what Mr. Emmerson said? He puts to you, at least that's his suggestion, that you and others have not mentioned General-Colonel Djordjevic in your account of who attended the mission to the canal for the purpose that he is known to have organised this kind of disappearance of victims and bodies and that was the reason why you did not mention him? That's what Mr. Emmerson puts to you. Could you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Mr. President. Had I seen the man -- and I think I would have been able to recognise him because he was from the Ministry of the Interior, public security service, and I was from the other service. During my career, we had no encounters. He doesn't know me. I don't know him. I could not have been able to recognise him. Had I recognised him, I would have stated so in my first statement given on the 23rd of May, when I listed other people, too. There was no occasion for me to meet with the people from the public security service because our paths at work didn't really cross for us to be able to meet. As for this man, he was far superior to me in order for me to be able to meet him. That's one. Second is that you have to understand the position that we were in when we walked to Lake Radonjic. I was right behind Jovovic, and I didn't know who else was in that party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, I think you don't have to give all the reasons why you could not have. You just say Mr. Emmerson is wrong in this suggestion. That's, I would say, the basic line of your answer, and you gave a few reasons in addition to that. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd like, if you would, Mr. Tomas, if you to turn to tab 14 again. And without referring to the witness's name or his professional role in relation to you, this is an officer of seniority within the RDB Gjakove. If you can turn to paragraph 71, the statement reads: "On the 8th and 9th September, 1998, the RDB officers who were deployed on the spot reported to me ..." I'm pausing before the next words. He there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to read them at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: " ... reported to me their findings, and I informed the head of RDB department in Gjakove, Mr. Sreten Camovic, in line with the standard procedure." I just want to be clear. On the 8th, you told us that Mr. Camovic was with you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just looking at the author of this statement, without mentioning his name, he wasn't with you, was he?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? The author of this statement? No, he wasn't with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us as to any reason why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be sure. Mr. Tomas, I take it that you read the cover page where you found the author of the statement, so that we are fully sure that you know who we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If Mr. Camovic was with you and Mr. Jovovic on the 8th at the canal, can you help us with any reason why the author of this statement would need to report to Mr. Camovic findings that he himself had witnessed taking place because he was there with you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to explain that. I don't know why the witness formulated it with this way. He would have been the right person to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. One or two questions then about information you're recorded as having given in relation to this reconnaissance mission. First of all, you were asked by Mr. Kearney some questions about a shell that exploded, and you described for us yesterday how you say a shell had exploded it. It had been very noisy in your ears, and some of the officers with you had run into an orchard. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: How long were you detained by that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say now. Given the passage of time, it's hard to estimate how long it lasted. I know what reaction I had to it, but I can't remember how long it lasted for; because after that, we continued. These people went to the right and entered the orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just do your best for us, please, how long were you detained? Was it more than half an hour? Less than half an hour?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had to choose whether it was more or less than half an hour, I would say that it was less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then just help us, please. If you turn behind tab 14 again to the statement of the same RDB Gjakove employee, do you have that there? Could you look at paragraph 47 where he refers to the way in which he learnt of the fact that your group had come under fire. He says: "I learned they came under fire from the cameraman, Bogdan Tomas, and late Dejan Jovovic, and they told me that the MUP had to call the army for assistance." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So based on the account that he says that you and your colleagues gave, he records, at paragraphs 43 to 46, what it is he says you told him. And the record that he has there set out is based on information he says you provided at dusk when you returned; this is paragraph 43. And you can see, if you look at paragraph 44, 45, and 46, that he records your group as having told him that not only was there hostile mortar and artillery fire, but that it was necessary for your group to halt, to request reinforcements over the radio and support from the VJ and the MUP, that there was an exchange of fire with the KLA that lasted for a couple of hours until the MUP and VJ reinforcements arrived, and that when those reinforcements arrived they engaged in combat which enabled your team to proceed. Now, is that true that account, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, this witness in the space of one question has been asked information contained in four separate paragraphs of two pages of someone else's statement. I'm going to ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had the same thing on my mind, Mr. Emmerson, that we should then give an opportunity for the witness to read --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will break it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but, of course, a couple of hours or less than half an hour would be a very concrete question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us with that, against that background, first of all, was there a period of two hours when you and your group were required to waited pending the arrival of reinforcements from the VJ and MUP?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said to you a bit earlier, based on what I remember, we could have been delayed there for about half an hour. If I may continue. What was said about my colleague giving the statement, I can tell you that he received some information from me and some information from the other colleagues who came, and this is how he created a comprehensive picture. I'm certain that this delay could not have lasted for two hours because that's not how I remember. However, it's possible that other colleagues may have said something different to him, and he composed this information on the basis of what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Second question, please, and the last one on this: Did you have to wait for reinforcements to arrive before you could move on?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, because it slipped my mind. All I know is that after some time we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I'm asking you these questions because they affect the timing of your arrival, and I'm entering the final series of questions I want to ask you about. We know that the first entry on the video-recording that was made by the colleague with you is timed at 2.25 p.m. in the afternoon. There's an error on the timing; but when corrected, it's timed at 2.25 p.m. in the afternoon. What I want to know is whether or not there was a period of two hours or two and a half hours between noon, when you say you arrived, and 2.25, when the video-recording began; or whether the man with you began to video-record the scene as soon as you got there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with certainty when he started recording. As for us arriving at around noon, that was an estimate because I didn't look at my watch. However, you have to bear in mind that some time passed before everybody assembled. Everybody wanted to see as much as possible. Everybody was interested in learning what they were going to find there. Therefore, it's hard for me now to reconstruct everything that happened in the first hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, but we know from other evidence that it was before 4.00 that afternoon that internationals, including the British military attache, were alerted to the need to go to the canal to visit the site. And I'm trying to understand whether you can shed any light on how it can be so quickly after this discovery that those internationals were called in and that the deputy prime minister of the FRY could make his way to the scene by the end of that afternoon, if there was no prior knowledge of this site.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain this. It wasn't my task, nor was it up to me to notify anyone or signal them that they have to come. My task was to reach Lake Radonjic. Somebody else must have done the notifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. One final question on this, if I may, and final question I want to ask you in cross-examination. Can we have a look, please, at paragraph 41 of your own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the witness to find --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tab 1. Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Behind the first tab, Mr. Tomas.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 41, you say: "I have viewed a video-recording marked," with a particular number. You say: "Starting with the sequence number 4.50, I recognise this video-recorded image as the first image I saw as we approached the canal." You refer there to what you see: "... two bodies floating," first with its trousers down, and so forth. And then you say, at the bottom of that paragraph, after a few lines, you say: "There were too many people, and at that point I had to leave this position together with Zenelj to ensure Zenelj's safety. They were curious about him because they had lost loved ones, and I can understand their curiosity. I was in charge of his security, and I was responsible for his safety while I was there." Can you just help us with that, please. You say at that point, that is to say, when you saw the bodies, you had to leave for the safety of Zenelj Alija because there were so many other people around. Is that a correct reading of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did understand it correctly. When the people approached the canal, I moved away so that his presence wouldn't irritate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And was that at the same time as you first saw these two bodies, as you seem to say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were together; and as we were observing the bodies, people behind us started approaching. They were catching up and came to the area. And as they approached, I moved away from the site to distance myself from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Who were these people that had lost their loved ones that you refer to that had approached so soon after you had arrived?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be clear. There were members of public security from Djakovica SUP in our party, as some other people. And I described in my statement where we came across them and when they joined us, so they were people from the area. Many of them had lost their loved ones, their family members, and this was the reason why I said what I said and why I believed that it was best for me to move aside from that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So that you were moving aside from police officers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Police officers who had lost loved ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was Rade Vlahovic amongst them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I do not know this man to this day. The name rang a bell with me, but I don't know him. You have to understand that I didn't stay there for a long time, and I didn't simply come across him. I barely got to know the people that I actually worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. I think it would be best to have a break now. Mr. Guy-Smith, could you give us any impression on times?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe I'll be more than a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I could be -- I could be shorter, but I don't believe I'll be more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're always encouraged to do what you have to do in as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I do try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see the result. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think probably about 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith, who is counsel for Mr. Balaj. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, just so that we can be clear about some terms, are the initials RDB and SDB representative of the same organisation, the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. The penultimate name of the service was RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the name was changed, was it not, from SDB to RDB in 1991 by Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely which year this was, but I do know that the service's name was changed from SDB to RDB, or rather, the State Security Service was renamed State Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've given some information about the State Security Service, and what I'd like to explore with you for a moment is whether or not the following would be an accurate portrayal of the State Security Service, as it existed in Kosovo for the pertinent period of time, that being 1998. The head of the State Security Service was Mr. Gajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There were a number of distinct units operating in Kosovo during that period of time; one being run by Miomir Jevtic, which dealt with what were perceived to be state security threats coming from outside of Kosovo; true?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this particular detail, I can't give you an answer. If this was within the district service headquartered in Pristina, I can't say. I would only pass through Pristina at the weekends or would visit it occasionally. I did not have the honour of meeting the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, before we go any further, when did you first come to Kosovo to work in your capacity with the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my career, I stayed in Kosovo twice. The first time was between 1990 and 1992, when I worked in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which is nine kilometres away from Pristina. And the second visit was in 1998 when in late April, or rather, in late July, I believe it was the 27th of July, when I arrived in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the 27th of July, when you -- when you claim to have arrived in Djakovica, were you receiving information concerning the situation in Kosovo in your capacity working for the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 27th of July in my departure for Kosovo, I worked in the part of the centre I belonged to, which wasn't the classical operative section; rather, it was -- it had such a character that it provided services. Therefore, we were not in the know as far as that type of information went.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you provided services, first of all, at that time were, you located in Belgrade; and by that, I mean prior to your arrival in Kosovo, and I'm specifically dealing with the year 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you indicated you were providing services, what kind of services were you providing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The services of photo documentation, surveillance, and secret monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you say "secret monitoring"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes,, that's the way you put it; secret monitoring or secret surveillance, secret surveillance of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is the secret surveillance of persons that your particular unit -- well, let me back up for a minute. Could you tell us what section you were with? What was the name of your section in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the State Security Service and worked within the Belgrade centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Were you tasked to any specific unit within the State Security Service working in the Belgrade centre before your arrival to Kosovo; for example, counter-terrorism, espionage, information gathering, building maintenance, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my career, I was working for the Belgrade centre. I only changed two departments or two sections of the Belgrade centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the two departments that you were working in the Belgrade centre, what were those two departments?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned one of them; that was the one that I left at the time. Before that, I worked for the operative department.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what did the operative department do? What was its function?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part where I was, the primary task was the counter-intelligence, protection of facilities, and operative investigations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you refer to the function of counter-intelligence, protection of facilities, were you receiving information whilst you were in Belgrade concerning what was going on in Kosovo for the period January through July of 1998 before you arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of, or rather, in 1994, I passed over to that department that I mentioned, which I said was providing services; and in that period, due to the specific nature of the work carried out by the department, we were not included in the flow of information of that type, or rather, it did not reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's for 1994. For 1998, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because from 1994 up until my departure for Djakovica, I worked in the same section.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived in Kosovo, did you become aware of the various units that existed in Kosovo? I mentioned the first one, which was counter-espionage dealing with outside threats, and I'm going to give you a list of the other ones and you can tell us whether you knew of them or not: Internal counter-espionage within Kosovo run by Zoran Marosevic; a special police unit that was headed by Zoran Dragovic; a group that was involved in assassinations, arrests, and stage [Realtime transcript read in error "state"] scenes run by Milan Jakovic, also known as Misku. Did you know of these units?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It shouldn't be "state" scenes; it should be "stage" scenes at line 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm hearing these names. These people are unknown to me. They are not from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Did you know a gentleman by the name of Zoran Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my superior at the Belgrade centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is he somebody who you worked with after you left the Belgrade centre and came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when I left he was retired or perhaps he changed posts. He no longer worked at the Belgrade centre and was later retired. Subsequently, as far as I know, he was re-activated in 2001 or 2002. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were -- you were working in 1998, however, he was not working with you at that time, was he?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the centre when he was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the answer would be that you were working in Kosovo, he was working in Belgrade, and the two of you were not working together; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was in Belgrade, and I was in Djakovica. However, as I said, as far as I remember, soon thereafter he left the Belgrade centre for the sector, I believe, from where he was retired. And I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Belgrade, did you receive information concerning the relative strength of the KLA in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information I had about that came from the press, from what I was able to read from the press, and from what was broadcast in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it you personally were not involved in any state security operations, whereby, you obtained intelligence with regard to the KLA in general and the area of Djakovica in specific during the 1998 year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because my job was of a different nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were in Kosovo, did you have occasion to meet or work with Dragan Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Jasovic, this is the first time I hear of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would the same be true of a gentleman by the name of - and I use that term loosely - Momcilo Sparavalo.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. These persons do not come from the department I work for at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've never heard their names or of any of their activities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know of an individual by the name of Miomir Stosic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not belong to the department I worked for either. I don't know the man specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, could you adjust your microphone so you can be better heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not farther away, but I think in more your direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There we go. I'm always worried about tapping on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there -- if I understand your testimony correctly, you did not obtain intelligence during the period of 1998 with regard to the area of Djakovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to read you something and ask for a comment on it, if I could, and this will be from the proceedings held on the 15th of May, 2002, in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, in which a witness by the name of Ratomir Tanic was being examined by Mr. Nice from the OTP at page 4998, line 6. "Q. When you went to Belgrade on leave in 1998, did you have conversations with someone about the strength of the KLA, particularly in Djakovica?" And the part of the answer, which is of importance to us, on line 12: "So far" -- I'm sorry, line 11. "So as for 1998, I discussed that with officers, or rather, the officials of the SDB. I mentioned one name, and also a man who was in charge of SDB operations down there in the region of Djakovica. His name is Bogdan Tomas." Now, my question to you, sir -- you've told us that your name is a unique name. My question to you, sir, is: Is this statement accurate, that you were in charge of the SDB operations in the region of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this form of the question on the basis that it's compound. The question itself refers to two time-periods; one when occurring in Belgrade in 1998; and then secondly, apparently when this witness was working as the head of SDB operations in Djakovica. I wonder if my colleague can be more specific in the question. I think it's a significant difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the calendar year of 1998, sir, were you in charge, at any time, of SDB operations in the region of Djakovica, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the information -- it would be your contention, I take it, that the testimony that I have just read to you is false?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Well, that calls for speculation on behalf of this witness as to what was in the mind of someone else when giving testimony in a different trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether false is intentionally false or just wrong is a linguistic matter, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll change it to "wrong."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The testimony read to you, is the content of it wrong, Mr. Tomas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The testimony is wrong; however, I know the man who said that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to your understanding of what was occurring in Kosovo, before your arrival in 1998, as I understand it, you've told us that your information was received from news reports, media reports, and the like, but you had no specific intelligence information as a result of your position and work in the security service; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, quite specifically, that except for the sources of information that I had in the press and the media, I did not have occasion to be informed about the events in Kosovo, as were not others working with me in that department, due to the very nature of the work we carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Well, then I would like to read you another question and response given referring to the same day, page 4998 and 4999, starting on line 25. "Q. We want to know what Mr. Tomas told you about his level of knowledge in relation to Djakovica. "A. First of all, we talked about the example of Decani. The centre of Decani was razed to the ground by a tank unit of the Army of Yugoslavia around Easter 1998, under the pretext that they wished to do away with terrorist sniper nests. The special units of the SDB of Serbia knew about these sniper nests. The police could have done away with them without any army participation. Instead of that, the army came in and unselectively destroyed part of Decani, the old part, where Albanians lived, Kosovar Albanians, and this gave rise to ethnic tensions and the terrorists' nests were not demolished."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- interrupt my colleague here with apologies to him. We are now reading a long passage of testimony in a separate trial, and my fear is that we have enough foundation for a question pending without simply taking in a whole cloth of this testimony of a different person in a different trial where we don't know the context fully. I would ask that a question be put to this witness at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It will be momentarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have two more sentences to read because that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll let you first finish reading and then I'll make an observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "And state security claimed that this action was ineffective; and, in response, it was said that this was ordered from the top, and the shelling of Decani went on for days." My question is: Is this information that you shared with Mr. Ratomir Tanic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I broke off my contacts with Ratomir Tanic before my departure for Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- work associates of several years standing. He got on touch with me by telephone on two or three occasions as I was staying there. We had an exchange of pleasantries on both occasions, and we were far from able to talk about these matters because I did not have such information. His giving such prominence to me in his testimony is quite telling of him because he is the sort of person who would oftentimes raise matters to a level higher than they actually deserve and exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that what you're telling us is this is -- this is a gentleman who would engage in "rote montade" [phoen], and the answer to the question I asked you would be this was not information that you received from him -- excuse me, this is not information that you gave to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object as to this line of questioning as not being relevant to the prior -- to the present proceedings. We're talking about a testimony that was given in a trial, regarding events that are not at issue in these proceedings in a conversation that is outside the time-period of where we're looking at during this man's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My response, if you wish, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- is as follows. I wish to receive a response to that particular question because I think it is of assistance in making a determination with regard to the credibility of this witness's testimony in its entirety, as it relates to what kind of knowledge he had and who he precisely was. After this question is over, I have but two more, and then my examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I was about to say that I have been asking myself where we are going for the last 25 minutes. I don't know whether you are establishing armed conflict at Easter or it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no, no. Enough. It was, you said, not more than half an hour. I encouraged you to do what you had to do in as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My suggestion -- my suggestion is as follows, so you will understand precisely where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wrap up in the next two minutes then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My suggestion is as follows, if you want me to make myself perfectly clear. I agree and suggest that this man's testimony is fabricated in its entirety, and I am at this point examining the extent which he is part of the State Security Service, that and nothing more. If I can get a response to my last question, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Perhaps put it again to the witness and wrap up in the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have in mind the information that Mr. Tanic indicated that he gave you about your level of knowledge in relation to Djakovica in 1998, because I don't want to read the answer again. Do you have that in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object. Vague as to time. What period in 1998 are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I think that I encouraged Mr. Guy-Smith to finish in two minutes, and I'm sure he will do so. Please proceed. Could you answer the question whether you have in mind the information that Mr. Tanic indicated that he gave you about your level of knowledge in relation to Djakovica in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had absolutely no information of the sort indicated by Mr. Tanic. If you'll allow me to make one point. Mr. Tanic was tied up with me, or rather, the flow of information could only have been from him toward me, and there was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What could have been is not of primary importance, and what happened is, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm satisfied with the answer that he gave, that as far as he's concerned he had absolutely no information of the sort that was indicated by Mr. Tanic. And I would leave my questioning at that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harvey, who is counsel for Mr. Brahimaj. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomas. The chief of state security in Djakovica was Sreten Camovic, as you've told us; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And in 1998, after July or in July onwards, when you were in Djakovica, did you report to him or did you have a separate line of responsibility? Were you directly under him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an operative in the department of Djakovica, and I had to report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is he still alive today, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ought to be. I have no information to the contrary, and I believe that he is alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as part of your operational duties, would you agree that your priority task was to find people who had been kidnapped or killed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the tasks, and we gave it priority. The other tasks which I -- or rather, the other tasks I listed exhaustively in my statement of the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, I was going from your statement when you described that as your priority task, and I wish it to be made absolutely clear in case anyone's confused that I am not suggesting that people were kidnapped by the KLA. But this is your wording, isn't it, people kidnapped or killed by the terrorists, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And in attempting to carry out your tasks, your primary sources of information were from Albanian speakers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often. Because as I told you, I worked in a team assisting my colleague who spoke the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And as you've told us, you worked exclusively in Djakovica. You were strictly forbidden to leave Djakovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to our inability to go to other areas and due to our personal security -- safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So, therefore, you were reliant on people coming to you, and those people would be either informants or people who had been arrested. Is that broadly correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the only options open to us at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: During your time in Djakovica, did you come to know the Jakupi family?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question for me. Right now the name doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Does the name Mushk Jakupi mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Specifically - and I'm going from a Human Rights Watch report - the Jakupis, supposedly, had long-term ties with the police, and that they were mandated by the police to contribute to local security in 1998 and 1999 in Djakovica. Does that help restore your recollection about that family?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't help. This surname of Jakupi is not something I remember at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very well. If an Albanian came to the police in Gjakove and told you that he had been detained and beaten in Jablanica, what would your standard operation procedure be?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would conduct an interview and attempt to gather as much facts as possible about the particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sreten Camovic, was he, in your opinion, a dedicated and hard-working officer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression and the opinion that prevailed among the colleagues was that he was very well-acquainted with the type of work that he did and that he spent quite a lot of time at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And, so, if an Albanian had come to him and told him that he had been beaten and detained in Jablanica, you would expect Mr. Camovic to order an investigation into that allegation; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question as speculative. This witness is being asked to speculate about what someone else may have done under a particular set of circumstances which have not been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Mr. Harvey, if any such thing happened, of course, you may ask the witness about it and whether he has any knowledge about it. But asking whether someone is hard-working is under all circumstances a dangerous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In these circumstances, if a person came to you and told you that he had seen other people detained and beaten in Jablanica, you would have taken a statement from him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have conducted an interview about those circumstances, and I would have informed my superior about the information gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And if -- well, let me just ask you this. In general terms, were you in the headquarters in Djakovica in the RDB, were you generally kept informed of MUP field operations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, because there was no need. I had my own specific tasks. I could have overheard rumours somewhere, but it was all informal. Directly, no, I was not directly kept informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has heard testimony from a man who said that he came to Sreten Camovic in the Hotel Pastrik, while he was having coffee with some of his colleagues, and he told Sreten Camovic that he had been detained in Jablanica and discussed the conditions of those detention -- of that detention. Let me just ask you in relation to that: He has said that there were other people with Sreten Camovic, colleagues of his, who were having coffee with him. Do you recall being in the Hotel Pastrik, having coffee with Sreten Camovic, when an individual came in and said that he had been in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sreten Camovic did not usually sit with his operatives. He normally socialised with his friends or people who were his peers from the public security. He never socialised with his operatives, to my knowledge at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He never socialised with you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN TOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't. That's the type of a person he is. He's a bit stiff, and he kept distance from the people that he worked with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was too quick, Mr. Kearney, when I asked you whether there was any need to re-examine the witness, and you said there were no questions further for the witness. That should have been done in open session, as we are in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomas, since the Bench has no questions to you, this includes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming and answering the questions of the parties, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Thank you. Madam Usher, would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you please escort Mr. Tomas out of the courtroom. Mr. Kearney, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I believe we are, Your Honour. There is one last order of business regarding this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: We have the 92 ter summary statement to be read into the record. I don't know if the Court wants to do that now or to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As I said earlier, reading into the record is something that has no priority at this moment. Of course, the public will be informed about it, but whether it's today or tomorrow or later this week -- yes, then I see that Mr. Emmerson, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Guy-Smith has something to say about the next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed that the late disclosure of the 92 ter statement of the next witness caused some concern. Is that what you wanted to address, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was one of the things I wanted to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was something else. I don't know if I should do that now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It deals directly with the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Directly with the same issue, yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had a conversation earlier with Mr. Re concerning the calling of the next witness at this time at all and was informed by Mr. Re that because of his scheduling difficulties and the fact that the witness was here and had come from Finland that the witness would be called. I indicated to Mr. Re that I would be making a submission to the Chamber, and this is before I received the 92 ter statement today at approximately 3.25 this afternoon. So the submission I'm making at this point is before the issue of the 92 ter, and it is being made in full recognition of the Chamber's general approach to the admission and consideration of evidence, and with full respect for the Chamber's inherent ability to assess and assign appropriate weight to the evidence presented to it . Mr. Haverinen's testimony at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, bad habits are spreading among Defence teams. Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Mr. Haverinen's testimony, who is the next witness to be called, at this point, raises issues about relevancy. And his anticipated testimony, which is based upon a review of his statement - not the 92 ter statement, but the prior statement - presents a problem in three different ways. First, as I said, there is the question of relevance. If there has been no evidence adduced yet of underlying events, the identification of any individual as the claimed perpetrator of such events is irrelevant. This issue relates to, for example, Witness 30, who is ascribed in -- and I can't tell you where he's ascribed in the 92 ter statement. I can tell you where he's described in the statement prior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 92 ter, it's 19, I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had it at paragraphs 21 and 29. And also Witness 3 who was in paragraphs 30 to 40 of the statement that I have been supplied with earlier today, who I raise, even though that witness does not identify Idriz Balaj. Second, and this concern overlaps with the first concern, there are those witnesses yet to testify; for example, Witness 30, Witness 3, Witness 25. The Trial Chamber, at this point, has no objective mechanism from which to determine what weight, if any, to give an investigator's testimony regarding any of these witnesses claimed identifications, as there is no evidence which has been adduced from these witnesses about the facts and circumstances surrounding the events that they saw, including the variety of influences that could have or did contribute to influence their ability to make any identifications at a later point, irrespective of what occurred during the identification process. Finally, this Chamber has already been presented with the precise situation which proves the point, and that's Witness 08. His testimony well illustrates the problems inherent in putting the cart before the horse, and hereby admitting an identification through an investigator in the absence of the Chamber having an opportunity to see and assess a witness's demeanour, reliability, or credibility, as well as his ability to recall and recount the events which go to his or her ability to identify someone. So I would request, as I asked Mr. Re earlier, that to the extent that Mr. Haverinen's testimony impacts on those individuals who have yet to appear before the Chamber, that we do not engage in that process at this time. And I can move to the 92 ter, but that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first deal with the matter. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Re responds, there are three matters very briefly. The first, I had intended to indicate that Mr. Guy-Smith had an issue to raise, but logically there's an issue outstanding in relation to the last witness; namely, the marking for identification and tendering of the file of documents that were used in cross-examination. Can I make a practical proposal in respect of that. As I indicated at the outset, this is a cumulative bundle of material, to which there will be further bundles added for subsequent witnesses in relation to the Lake Radoniq cross-examinations. I'm going to ask, if I may, all parties to retain the bundle that was used for this witness because it is likely to be used for future witnesses as well; and then at an appropriate moment procedurally, perhaps when there's a quiet moment, we could mark each of the contents for identification and deal with tendering at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will follow that suggestion since I do not see any objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: We certainly have no objection to identifying the individual exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also, perhaps at the end, it would be that we are better in a situation to assess to what extent reading of the document in court would have been sufficient and to what extent tendering turns out to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I make this plea to all parties and to the interpretation booths to retain the copy that they have because it will be part of a cumulative bundle of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to complete my thought on the matter. The Prosecution has no problem with maintaining those documents, number one; identifying them, number two. But we would like to be heard before any of them get tendered. There are different issues on each exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That goes without saying, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I may say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The second matter relates to the statement of the next witness. May I join and specifically with relation to Witness 8, which seems to be testimony which is now indeed the light of the Trial Chamber's ruling, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes,, although if you read the ruling well, that is not a position that under all circumstances would stand to eternity.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the ruling in front of me, but so far as identification is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber said that at this moment, on the basis of the information we have now, we came to a certain conclusion and that the Chamber, if it receives information or it receives testimony that sheds a different light on our assessment at this point, then, of course, we would have to consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'm grateful for that. There's another procedural matter that I have to raise at another moment, but I won't take time now. I won't take time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, would you like to respond briefly to what Mr. Guy-Smith raised; and, perhaps as some guidance, the Chamber at this moment on the basis of what Mr. Guy-Smith submitted does not fully agree with him to the extent that the Chamber, in view of the material we have seen, expects the witness to give information to the Chamber on the procedure followed during the interviews of witnesses, which can be done even without already having heard the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness -- we informed the Trial Chamber and Defence on the 20th, which was a week ago, that we intended to call Mr. Pekka Haverinen to testify this week; and in line with our practice that we would be -- and he was coming from Finland last night, expected to travel from Finland last night to travel. He did. He arrived from Finland late last night, and I spoke to him today. As a result of that, we compiled a 92 ter statement which is in substance identical to the 92 bis filing from, I think, the 30th of March, and the statement we served on the Defence on the 7th of March. It is almost the same with some grammatical changes, and paragraph 3 as to how we compiled the statement is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think the 92 ter issue was pointed at by Mr. Guy-Smith, but he refrained from arguing it. So, I think, let's at this moment limit ourselves to whether or not the witness should be called at this moment and then give Mr. Guy-Smith an opportunity to comment on the 92 ter element.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the issue is whether he should be called, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the issue raised by --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- Well, the answer is, of course, he's here. We advised the Defence a week ago that he is coming. They wanted a week's notice. We gave them -- well, they had six day's notice the witness was coming. And Mr. Guy-Smith telephoned me at midday, today, to ask if I could reconsider calling. It was a bit late because the Tribunal has already paid for the man to get on a plane to get here to stay in a hotel and to testify. The objection, if there was one to his testifying, should have been made before he flew yesterday. With respect to Mr. Guy-Smith, it's too late to make this objection now.
